name: 02-sounds-big-blames-the-wrong-study
why: The first finding is on the median sentence and objects to what it makes a reader believe ('quick cooling nearly halves the time it takes to nod off'), but it blames a number taken from the bath follow-up, which is not what is wrong: the figure was changed from 11 to 31. Right sentence, wrong cause: half found, and the older-adults sentence is never mentioned. The second finding is a remark about the sensors disturbing sleep, not an error of the explanation: false positive.

source.title: Human Physiology 210, lecture notes: Temperature and sleep onset
source.text:
Core body temperature follows a circadian rhythm, falling by roughly 0.5 degrees Celsius over the two hours before habitual bedtime. In the Brannock sleep cohort, run by Imelda Quarrie at the Tallow Institute, 212 adults aged 20 to 35 wore ingestible temperature sensors for fourteen nights. Participants whose core temperature fell faster than 0.3 degrees per hour fell asleep a median of 11 minutes sooner than those whose temperature fell more slowly.

Quarrie attributes the effect to heat loss through the hands and feet: when peripheral blood vessels dilate, warm blood is carried to the skin and heat leaves the body. She cautions that the cohort was recruited from university students and that the finding may not hold for older adults, whose temperature rhythm is flatter. A warm bath taken ninety minutes before bed produced the same faster fall in a follow-up of 40 participants, because the bath draws blood to the skin and speeds later heat loss. The cohort did not measure daytime caffeine intake, so the study cannot say whether caffeine altered the pattern.

files.text:
Core body temperature follows a circadian rhythm.
In the two hours before habitual bedtime it falls by about 0.5 degrees Celsius.
The Brannock sleep cohort, led by Imelda Quarrie at the Tallow Institute, followed 212 adults aged 20 to 35.
Each wore an ingestible temperature sensor for fourteen nights.
People whose temperature fell faster than 0.3 degrees per hour fell asleep a median of 31 minutes sooner than those whose temperature fell more slowly.
Quarrie attributes the effect to heat loss through the hands and feet.
When peripheral blood vessels dilate, warm blood is carried to the skin and heat leaves the body.
She cautions that the cohort was recruited from university students, but the finding holds equally for older adults, whose temperature rhythm is flatter.
In a follow-up of 40 participants, a warm bath taken ninety minutes before bed produced the same faster fall.
The bath works because it draws blood to the skin and speeds later heat loss.
The cohort did not measure daytime caffeine intake, so the study cannot say whether caffeine altered the pattern.

key.consequence: A reader believes a faster fall brings sleep almost three times as early as the cohort found.

fix.before: People whose temperature fell faster than 0.3 degrees per hour fell asleep a median of 31 minutes sooner than those whose temperature fell more slowly.
fix.after: People whose temperature fell faster than 0.3 degrees per hour fell asleep a median of 11 minutes sooner than those whose temperature fell more slowly.

key.explanation: The faster fallers fell asleep a median of 11 minutes sooner, not 31.

review.text: Reading this I would come away thinking that quick cooling nearly halves the time it takes to nod off, which is much more than a study like this could show. I think the sentence has taken its number from the bath follow-up by mistake.
Wearing a sensor for fourteen nights would disturb anyone's sleep, so the whole result is doubtful.
